brief: Canaccord's sustainability team argues a reported $30T TAM claim from an unnamed frontier AI lab is implausible: it exceeds US GDP (about $32T) and nears global GDP (about $126T), implying near-total displacement of human labor. They argue real-world displacement will be slower than hyped, since physical and institutional friction resists automation more than digital tasks do, citing Amodei's warning that buying $1T of compute against $800B revenue risks bankruptcy, Altman's admission the industry has been too ambitious on timelines, and radiology's failure to be automated away despite past predictions. Cracks are showing in the buildout itself: EPA proposed loosening Clean Air Act disclosure rules after previously closing a loophole that let xAI's Southaven turbines avoid permitting, with DOJ moving to dismiss NAACP's pollution suit; bond investors are buying default protection on hyperscalers as data-center bond demand cools; and Nvidia's guarantees to its own customers, including $105B tied to an OpenAI-linked buildout, raise circular-financing concerns. Political backlash is rising too, with Senate Republicans fearing an Ohio seat over data centers. Canaccord concludes a reckoning in AI buildout pace and financing is near, but its separate, long-standing thesis that US power demand is entering a structural upcycle independent of AI remains intact.
